feedback: Check each arrow's tail touches the object — a piece lying away from the object has no clear owner.
If both pieces are the same length when the forces differ, ask which force should be bigger and swap in a longer piece.
When two objects interact, confirm the learner has drawn only the forces on the single chosen object, not forces that object exerts on others.
activities.intendedInsight: A force diagram is a representation of one chosen object with the forces acting ON it; building it physically makes the replacement principle and arrow attachment concrete before committing to pencil.
learnerActions: Use physical 'cardboard arrows' (cut to different lengths) laid onto a picture or model of one object to build up its force diagram before drawing on paper.
Place each arrow so its tail sits on the object and point it the way the force acts; pick a longer piece for a bigger force.
For a pair of interacting objects, build the diagram for ONE object at a time, replacing the other object with the force arrow it exerts.
Describe out loud which object each arrow acts on and name the force type.
activities.title: Cardboard arrows: build the diagram by hand first

feedback: Box: the arrows are opposite and the push is longer, so forces are unbalanced with a resultant to the right — and because the box is already moving right, it speeds up.
Resting book: draw two arrows ON the book — weight DOWN and the table's support force UP — equal in length (balanced), both starting on the book, so it stays still.
If nothing is drawn on the book: a still book has weight down and the table pushing up, equal and opposite — balanced does not mean absent.
If only the weight is drawn: the table also pushes up on the book; without it the book would not stay still.
Equal push and friction → balanced → no change in motion, so the box keeps moving right at the steady speed it already had.

Friction longer than push → resultant to the left → the rightward-moving box slows down and comes to a stop. It does NOT reverse: sliding (kinetic) friction only opposes the box's current rightward slip, so it cannot by itself drive the box backward. Once the box stops, reassess the forces: kinetic friction no longer acts, but the rightward push is still present and is now balanced by static friction, so the box stays at rest rather than reversing or re-accelerating. Reversal would need a sustained non-friction force pushing left.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a diagram: the longer opposing arrow sets the resultant's direction → unbalanced → the motion changes that way relative to how the box is already moving. Constructing a diagram: even a still object has forces — weight down AND the table's support (normal) force up, equal and opposite (balanced), both starting on the book — so 'still' is drawn with balanced arrows, not a blank.
learnerActions: Look at a force diagram of a box being pushed to the right across the floor (already moving right): a long arrow right labelled 'push' and a shorter arrow left labelled 'friction'. State what the lengths and directions tell you about what the box is doing.
Identify the resultant's direction and justify it from the arrow lengths.
Draw the force arrows for a book resting still on a table, attaching each arrow to the book and labelling it.
Redraw the box with push and friction EQUAL and say what the box is now doing.
Answer: if the friction arrow became longer than the push, what would happen to the box that is moving right?
activities.title: Interpret and construct: the resting book and the pushed box

feedback: Reject 'must be stationary' when the object is already moving: balanced forces mean no change in motion, which includes constant-speed gliding.
For a mid-air arrow, reattach its tail to the object and confirm which object the force acts on.

When identifying the resultant, confirm it points in the direction of the net force and is drawn as a single arrow. For two opposite arrows, that is the way of the longer arrow. For several arrows along one line, add up the arrows pointing each way and compare the totals; the longest single arrow does not always win. Then state how the resultant changes the object's motion relative to how it is already moving.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent learners consistently attach arrows to the object, read length as magnitude and direction as the way the force acts, and know balanced forces can accompany steady motion, not only rest.
learnerActions: Error-finding: given a diagram, spot the arrow that does not start on the object ('spot the mid-air arrow') and redraw it correctly.
Choose from outcomes for 'balanced or unbalanced — what happens next?', including a 'must be stationary' option to be rejected when the object is already moving.
Match each diagram to its motion description.
Identify the resultant for a given pair or set of arrows.
Sketch the arrows onto a pictured object for a described situation, stating the object's current motion.
activities.title: Spot the error / match the motion (quick checks)
